bloques.html:
Read the story and answer questions 6 to 10.

The Blue Ribbon

The gym was a beehive that Saturday, buzzing with parents and poster boards. When the judge pinned the blue ribbon on my project, my hands shook, and not from joy.

Three nights earlier, I had found the mistake. My bean plants under red light had not grown twice as fast as the others. I had measured them in centimeters one week and in inches the next, and the numbers I was so proud of were wrong. Fixing it meant starting over, and the fair was in three days. So I closed my notebook and told myself that nobody would ever check.

Nobody did. The judge smiled. My little brother clapped until his hands turned pink. Dad took eleven photos. The ribbon should have felt light as a feather, yet it sat in my pocket like a stone.

I looked across the gym at Tomás, who had come second. For two months he had counted the ants in his yard every morning before school, even in the rain. He was folding his poster carefully, as if it still mattered.

My feet started walking before my head had decided anything. The judge was packing her bag.

"Excuse me," I said. My voice came out small. "There is something wrong with my data."

alternativas.html: Third person: a narrator outside the story reports the thoughts of every character.
First person: the narrator is a character, so the reader knows her thoughts but not the thoughts of the judge or Tomás.
First person: the narrator is Tomás, who is watching the winner.
Third person: a narrator outside the story follows only Dad.

bloques.html: Which statement correctly describes the point of view of "The Blue Ribbon"? (1 pt)

pauta.respuesta: B) First person: the narrator is a character, so the reader knows her thoughts but not the thoughts of the judge or Tomás

Read the poem and answer questions 11 to 13.

Night Train

The night train is a needle, threading
dark hills to darker hills.
Its one bright eye goes hunting
for the place where the track ends.

Inside, a hundred strangers sleep
like letters in an envelope,
each one addressed to a different morning.

Only the whistle stays awake,
calling out the names of towns
nobody on board will ever see.

Join these two sentences into one sentence that contains a relative clause with who. Do not use "and". (2 pts)

The judge was packing her bag. The judge had pinned the ribbon on my project.

pauta.respuesta: Modelo: The judge, who had pinned the ribbon on my project, was packing her bag. También vale: The judge who was packing her bag had pinned the ribbon on my project. Las comas son correctas en el primer modelo, pero no se exigen. 2 pts: una sola oración, con cláusula relativa con who pegada a "the judge", sin repetir "the judge" y sin "and". 1 pt: cláusula relativa presente pero con un error (usa which o that, repite "the judge", o el verbo queda mal). 0: une con "and" o deja dos oraciones

pautaHtml:
Guion de Listening (leer dos veces, en voz alta)

Lee a ritmo normal, como una escritora que habla ante un curso. Pausa de 30 segundos entre lecturas. No expliques palabras. La autora y su novela son inventadas: texto creado para esta prueba.

Author's Corner: Who Tells the Story?

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for inviting me. People often ask me where my ideas come from. Today I want to talk about a harder question: who should tell the story?

My novel is about a storm that cuts off a small island for nine days. In my first draft, a narrator outside the story told everything. That narrator knew what every character was thinking. It was accurate, but my editor said it felt like watching the storm through a window.

So I rewrote the whole book in the voice of Inés, who is eleven and is the lighthouse keeper's daughter. Now the reader only knows what Inés knows. When her father goes out in the boat, we do not know if he is safe, because she does not know. Readers tell me that is the chapter where they cannot stop reading.

I lost something, too. I could no longer show what the father was thinking, and I had to cut two chapters I loved. But a story is not a report. I did not want my readers to be informed about the storm. I wanted them to be inside it.

So when you write this week, try your story twice, with two different narrators. Then keep the one that makes your reader hold their breath.

Guion de Speaking (4-5 minutos)

Solo en inglés. El niño puede mirar el cuento. No corrijas durante la conversación; anota y califica al final con la rúbrica. En el paso 4 tomas a propósito la postura contraria a la suya: se evalúa cómo responde, no si te convence.

  1. Warm-up (30 s, no se califica): "What are you reading at the moment? Would you recommend it?"
  2. Summary (1 min): "Summarize 'The Blue Ribbon' in about five sentences. Tell me who the narrator is, what her problem is and what she decides." Apoyo: "What happened three nights before the fair?" / "How does the story end?"
  3. Opinion with reasons (1-2 min): "Should the judge let her keep the blue ribbon? Give me two reasons, and use one detail from the story as evidence." Apoyo: "Which words in the story make you think that?"
  4. Objection (1 min): si dijo que sí debe conservarla: "But she hid the mistake for three days and only confessed after she had won. Why should that be rewarded?" Si dijo que no: "But she told the truth when nobody would ever have found out. Isn't that worth more than a correct measurement?" Deja que responda sin interrumpir.
  5. Cierre: "Thank you, that's all."

Rúbricas

Escritura (ítem 17) — 1 punto por criterio cumplido. Valen las dos posturas (es valiente / no lo es); lo que se califica es la prueba.

Criterio 1 pt si...
Claim, reasons and evidence: postura La primera oración responde la pregunta y da una razón (She is brave because...)
Claim, reasons and evidence: cita Incluye al menos una cita exacta del cuento, entre comillas, que tiene que ver con su postura
Explicación Una oración explica cómo la cita apoya la postura (no se limita a repetirla) y hay oración de cierre
Lenguaje 4 a 6 oraciones completas, al menos una oración compleja (because, although, when, who...), máximo 2 errores de ortografía o puntuación

Respuesta modelo: The narrator is brave, although she is not brave at the beginning. For three days she hides her mistake and tells herself that "nobody would ever check." However, when she sees Tomás folding his poster, she walks to the judge and says, "There is something wrong with my data." These words cost her the ribbon, and she says them even though nobody has asked. Telling a truth that only you know is the hardest kind of courage.

Speaking (ítem 18) — cada criterio 0, 1 o 2 puntos:

Criterio 2 pts 1 pt 0 pts
Resumen Dice quién narra, el error de medición, que lo ocultó y que al final lo confiesa, en orden y sin detalles de relleno Falta uno de esos cuatro elementos o se pierde en detalles No logra resumir

Qué mira este instrumento

Nivel Cambridge Primary English Stage 6 (inglés como primera lengua) y Common Core ELA Grade 5. Comprensión auditiva de una charla con preguntas de propósito e inferencia (1-5); análisis literario de un cuento en primera persona: punto de vista, efecto del lenguaje figurado, propósito de un detalle, tema y cita de evidencia (6-10); un poema: metáfora, símil y atmósfera (11-13); oraciones complejas y cláusulas relativas (14-16); párrafo con postura y evidencia (17); speaking de resumen, opinión justificada y respuesta a una objeción (18). El cuento, el poema y la charla son textos creados para esta prueba.

Control Mineduc: quedan cubiertos los OA de Inglés 5º de comprensión auditiva (OA1-4), comprensión de lectura (OA5-9), expresión oral (OA10-13) y escritura (OA14-16). Para este niño se dan por superados: los OA piden textos breves y simples con apoyo visual y aquí lee, escucha y escribe sin apoyo a nivel de hablante nativo de su edad.

Señales: si acierta 6 pero falla 7, 8 y 12, identifica el recurso pero no explica su efecto, que es justo lo que pide Stage 6. Si falla 9, confunde tema con asunto o con un detalle (alternativas A y C). Si en 10 copia bien pero no explica, le falta el tercer paso (claim → quote → explain); lo mismo se verá en el criterio "Explicación" del ítem 17. Si falla 14-16 pero escribe oraciones complejas en el 17, le falta el nombre de la estructura, no la estructura.

Si le fue mal

  • Efecto del lenguaje figurado: al leer juntos, detenerse en una comparación y preguntar "¿por qué eligió esto y no otra cosa?" (por qué una piedra y no una caja).
  • Tema: después de cualquier cuento o película, pedirle "dime en una oración qué dice esto sobre la vida" y descartar juntos las respuestas que son sólo el asunto.
  • Evidencia: jugar a "pruébalo": cada vez que opine sobre un personaje, pedir la frase exacta del texto y una oración que la explique.
  • Cláusulas relativas: darle pares de oraciones sobre personas de la familia para unir con who, whose y which.
  • Punto de vista: hacer la misión de la guía ("The narrator swap") con otra escena de un libro que esté leyendo.
